⁠

all_videos_in_window.description: It’s the time of year when tuna of all shapes and sizes command a huge portion of the New England angler’s brain. Rhode Island waters have seen good numbers of bonito this week and many of them are of the larger variety. raw_posts.title: Mon Aug 24 – Whale Watching
raw_posts.content: Today we sailed southeast to find cetaceans in an area where several humpbacks have been seen previously. On the way, we found two large groups of Tamanend’s bottlenose dolphins (at least 120-150 individuals each) which we shared an exceptional encounter with. Typically, Tamanend’s are relatively shy around our vessels and disappear beneath the surface when moving near us. These dolphins, however, remained adjacent to the Viking Star, porpoising, interacting, and circle feeding providing incredible views into this species’ daily lives. We continued south and came across an ocean sunfish, Mola mola, which was resting at the surface. The densest of all bony fish, this animal did not mind our presence and moved under the vessel from one side to the other, allowing everyone to observe this unique species! raw_posts.title: Sat Aug 22 – Whale Watching
raw_posts.content: Despite a light drizzle at the dock, we sailed away from Montauk under cloudy, but dry conditions, and found our first whale approximately three miles from shore. This was a minke whale, the smallest of baleen whales, which surfaced regularly around the vessel in short (30 seconds to 1.5 minutes) intervals while feeding on the rich abundance of bait (likely silversides) at the surface. Minkes are generally fast and elusive, so it was a treat to observe this cetacean within a small area with repeated, multiple views. We moved on and a few miles later encountered numerous pods of Tamanend’s bottlenose dolphin. After spending some time with the pods, we traveled several miles southeast in search of some of the humpbacks encountered on previous trips. raw_posts.content: Humpback moms and calves in action! Under clear skies and cool ocean breezes, the Viking Starship headed east in search of the whales that have been in the region all summer, but have recently spread out as bait has also been on the move. all_videos.description:
Everyone says striped bass go deep when the water warms — these fish clearly didn't get the memo. At 9am, in bright sun and 70-something degree water, dozens of stripers were cruising a Nantucket Sound flat in barely a foot of crystal-clear water. 

They were incredibly tough to fool, but just watching them glide through water that shallow was impressive. Anyone else found stripers recently somewhere they 'weren't supposed to be'? Drop a comment below — love to hear about it.
